draft.summary: [child] is making good progress in addition and is working on subtraction with larger numbers. [child] can add two-digit and three-digit numbers in columns, carrying when needed, and uses mental strategies like bridging through ten to work out sums and differences. Over these 26 days, [child] has improved in three-digit subtraction, getting more questions right on the recent papers than on earlier ones. Some slips with exchanging across a zero and counting tens are being worked on.

can_do.sentence: [child] adds two two-digit numbers in columns and in a line, carrying exactly when a column needs it.
[child] adds two three-digit numbers, carrying from any column, including onto a zero.
[child] works out sums and differences mentally by bridging through ten or using a friendly number, and finds what makes both sides of an equals sign balance.
[child] takes a one-digit number from a three-digit number, exchanging across a zero when it must.
[child] adds a one-digit number to a three-digit number, with the one-digit number under the ones.
[child] solves one- and two-step word problems, choosing each operation from what happens in the story rather than a keyword, and using the first answer in the second step.
[child] takes a two-digit number from a two-digit number, exchanging a ten for ten ones when the ones need it.
[child] adds a two-digit number to a three-digit number, with the numbers lined up by the ones.
[child] takes a three-digit number from a three-digit number, exchanging in any column, across one zero or several, and has improved from earlier papers to recent ones.

working_on.explanation: When counting back in tens, [child] sometimes counts one extra ten, making the answer ten more than it should be. The educator and [child] count back in tens on a hundred-square to check the answer and see where the count went.
When exchanging across a zero, [child] turns the zero into a nine correctly but then forgets to take from the hundreds. The educator uses a number line count-up as a check.
Sometimes [child]'s answer is one more than the correct total, likely from a number fact that is off by one. Number bonds and ten-frame practice help [child] build fluency with the facts.

at_home: Try the subtraction question beside this together: 306 − 128. After [child] works it out, count up from the answer on your fingers or with coins to check it reaches 306. This helps [child] notice when the exchange across the zero is correct.

Make a two-digit number together with ten-rupee and one-rupee coins, then take away a smaller two-digit number. Count the change together to check the answer. This gives [child] practice with exchanging and builds confidence in subtraction.

Play with number bonds: show [child] a number like ten, made with two groups of coins or objects, then hide one group and ask how many are hidden. Swapping which group you hide helps [child] see all the ways to make the number.

bad: [child] turns the zero into a nine correctly but then forgets to take from the hundreds

draft.summary: [child] is building strong foundations in addition and subtraction of two-digit numbers, and can work mentally with strategies like bridging through ten. Over these 24 days, [child] has shown real progress in three-digit subtraction, improving from earlier attempts. [child] is now working with three-digit numbers in addition and subtraction, and solving word problems that need two steps. The main things to watch are keeping track of all the steps in a problem, and remembering to reduce a column after exchanging a ten during subtraction.

can_do.sentence: [child] adds two two-digit numbers in columns and in a line, carrying exactly when a column needs it.
[child] works out sums and differences mentally by bridging through ten or using a friendly number, and finds what makes both sides of equals balance.
[child] takes a two-digit number from a two-digit number, exchanging a ten for ten ones when the ones need it.
[child] adds a one-digit number to a three-digit number, writing the one-digit number under the ones.
[child] takes a one-digit number from a three-digit number, exchanging across a zero when it must.

working_on.explanation: When [child] counts in tens during addition, the tens column sometimes goes one too high, making the answer ten more than it should be. The educator counts in tens on a hundred-square with [child] to keep track of exactly how many tens there are.

In the train question beside this, [child] found the answer to the first step but stopped there, instead of using it to answer the full question. The educator now asks [child] to underline both things that happen, and to use two boxes—one for each step.

When exchanging a ten in the subtraction beside this, [child] added the ten to the ones but forgot to reduce the tens column. The educator asks [child] to cross out and rewrite the tens digit before subtracting.

at_home: Try the kite question beside this together, and act it out with coins.

Make a three-digit number with [child] using three piles of rupee coins or buttons (one pile for hundreds, one for tens, one for ones). Take away a smaller three-digit number you choose. If you need to exchange, cross out and rewrite the tens digit before taking away.
Count up in tens together on paper or using coins. Start at different numbers and count: ten, twenty, thirty. This helps [child] notice when the tens are right, especially during longer additions.

draft.summary: [child] is learning to add two 2-digit numbers, and this skill has improved over these 26 days. [child] can add two 2-digit numbers in columns and in a line, carrying exactly when a column needs it. The educator has noticed that [child] is working through some common slips when adding: sometimes writing the full column sum instead of regrouping, sometimes being off by one in the answer, and occasionally dropping the carry when it comes out of the last column. With practice and the support the school is giving, [child] will build on these strengths. [child] has improved at adding two-digit numbers, and now gets them right every time.

can_do.sentence: [child] adds two 2-digit numbers in columns and in a line, carrying exactly when a column needs it, and this has improved from earlier answers to more recent ones.

working_on.explanation: When [child] adds, sometimes the full column sum gets written side by side instead of being regrouped into tens and ones. The educator uses ten-frames and rods to show that only one digit fits in each column.
Sometimes [child]'s answer comes out one more than the correct total. The educator is building number bonds and ten-frame fluency so [child] can check the size of the answer.

Occasionally the carry that comes out of the last column gets dropped, so the answer becomes too small. The educator asks [child] to estimate first, and checks: can the answer really be smaller than the bigger number we started with.

at_home: Try the question 69 + 25 together using coins or small objects. Make 69 with tens and ones, then add 25, and count what you have altogether. This helps [child] see what happens when you regroup.

Play with two-digit numbers using things at home like spoons, buttons or coins arranged in tens and ones. Take turns making a two-digit number and adding another one without writing it down, just by counting and grouping. Keep it to ten minutes or so.
When [child] adds numbers, ask: is the answer bigger than the bigger number we started with? This helps [child] check if the answer makes sense before writing it down.

bad: now gets them right every time
